name: Clifford Berry
milestone_by_age_26: Co-built and demonstrated the prototype Atanasoff-Berry Computer (ABC), the world's first electronic digital computer, in October 1939 at age 21, with a full-scale version completed by 1942.
early_history_summary: Berry graduated from Marengo High School as valedictorian at age 16 in 1934, having learned about electronics from his father's appliance repair shop. He studied electrical engineering at Iowa State College, earning a BS in 1939. That same year, physics professor John Vincent Atanasoff hired Berry as his graduate assistant to build the ABC prototype, which was first demonstrated in October 1939.
family_context_summary: Born in Gladbrook, Iowa to Fred and Grace Berry. His father owned an appliance repair shop where Berry learned about radios and electronics as a child. His father encouraged his tinkering with electricity.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father owned an appliance repair shop, providing Berry with early hands-on exposure to electronics and radio technology from childhood.
primary_early_advantage_tags: father appliance shop, electronics tinkering, Atanasoff mentor, ABC computer, valedictorian at 16, vacuum tubes
evidence_summary: Berry grew up in his father's appliance repair shop, learning electronics and radio technology from childhood. He graduated high school as valedictorian at 16 and earned a BS in electrical engineering from Iowa State College in 1939. That year, professor John Vincent Atanasoff specifically selected Berry as his graduate assistant to build the world's first electronic digital computer—the ABC—whose prototype was demonstrated in October 1939. The complementary Atanasoff-Berry partnership combined Atanasoff's conceptual vision with Berry's electronics and mechanical construction skills. The ABC was designated an IEEE Milestone in 1990.
starting_point: Born in Gladbrook, Iowa to Fred and Grace Berry; father owned an appliance repair shop where Berry learned about radios and electronics from childhood.
current_position: Died in October 1963 at age 45 in New York City; final role: computer scientist who co-created the Atanasoff-Berry Computer.
